Olifants: Cry Me A River

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Carte Blanche goes to Burgersfort where the Olifants river is rotten - filled with diapers and dead animals. We travel the river's path and investigate the reasons it's so polluted.

Unique Selling Point:
Diapers, diapers everywhere. The community of Burgersfort are superstitious and are throwing away diapers into the nearby Olifants river, so much so, that Peter Mashile who was raised in the community has decided enough is enough. He has employed several people to clean the diapers and give them back to the community's ready to reuse. Farmers in the area have lost cattle who have drunk the water and we speak to the mothers and ask why they do this. We will also speak to Peter who has fought to keep the river clean.
Award - are an NGO based in Hoedspruit they are studying the river and are finding a unique management system to help with the pollution. We will go with them and test the water in burgersfort, we will also interview their CEO about the project and the problems that the river is experiencing.

Summary:
We will chat to several experts along the river - Paul Oberholster from the CSIR who worked on the project of cleaning the river with the Olifants River Forum. They obtained a report that has never been published and they have given to Carte Blanche. They tried to fix the upper river and can explain why the lower parts are so polluted.

We will be flying over the Kruger National Park and seeing how dry it is, but also to get visuals - this will be with the bataleurs.

We will also speak to ecologist -and vetinarian Dr. David Huchzermeyer about the animals in the river - he is a fish expert and studied why the fish and crocodiles were being diagnozed with a rare disorder called Pansteatitis. He will explain how the river has had it's problems and with the drought it may get worse next year.

We have obtained several reports from Dr. Koos Pretorius on the acid mine drainage - where he says 30% of the river's ecology has been killed off. We also have other reports from a professor at University of Limpopo to back up the fish are dying throughout the system.

Press Release:


Cry Me a River
The Olifants River runs from Witbank into the Kruger National Park and is the only source of water for two million people, livestock and wildlife. But, it’s barely flowing. Thousands of soiled disposable nappies line its banks, blocking its natural course. Adding to the environmental and humanitarian disaster are raw sewage and mining effluent entering the river from its tributaries, seemingly unnoticed. Carte Blanche asks: how did the Olifants River become one of the country’s most polluted water sources?



Script:


These colours, reminiscent of a Jackson Pollock painting, are actually deceptive streams of toxic contaminants that have stained the Olifants river system.
The river is severely polluted, spelling disaster for the the Kruger National Park’s wildlife and the two million people who depend on it.
It spans a staggering 540 kilometers...
Link: The Olifants. A picturesque river that runs all the way from Witbank and beyond to the Ocean in Mozambique, but the water has to survive growing threats along the way, and for the thousands of people and the animal life that depend on it, the future is not looking good.
These smoggy coal mines in Mpumalanga are responsible for leaking acidic water into the water table through Acid Mine Drainage. It’s made the water as acidic as instant coffee at a PH of around 3.5, says CSIR Chief Water Scientist Dr. Paul Oberholster.
Paul: “We are the 6th largest producer of coal in the world. 50% of our power generation is coming from this catchment.”
Further downstream in the Loskop dam, locals use the water recreationally, blissfully unaware of the presence of the bio-toxin blue green algae.
Paul: “It’s an algae that forms mats on the water surface and it cause impact by reducing oxygen in the system, killing your fish life and possible other organism in the system.”
The river perserveres running into the middle of the Olifants catchment area, via the Steelpoort River through Burgersfort in Limpopo.
Here locals wash laundry, while their children fish mere meters away from hundreds of soiled nappies that litter the water’s edge. Worsened by the drought, low water levels reveal pools of sewage-laden algae and thousands of nappies.
All of these pollutants are washed into the lower Olifants catchment in Phalaborwa.
Working for AWARD, an NGO that tracks the Olifants’ water quality and flow, Scientist Thabo Mohlala has, for 10 years, tested this water. He’s found that three of Phalaborwa’s municipal sewage pumping stations aren’t fully functional.
Thabo: “So we have three, one is in the Namagala, another in the lulekane Township and the main one from town. At this point in time, they’re not properly working and they flow into the Selati river.
We visited the Namakgale Township where raw foamy effuent gushes from the leaking sewage pump station.
Thabo:” The sewage plant there was designed back in the years, so the station there as well can’t actually handle the current flow.”
The bacteria and sewage then flows into the Olifants via the Ga-Selati river, where downstream algal mats indicate the water’s toxicity.
Paul: “The cause of this is normally due to treated or untreated waste water.”
According to the 2016 South African Health Review, sewage-borne eColi bacteria that ends up in water causes diarrhoea, the third largest killer of children and the elderly in this country.
Phalaborwa’s main pumping station is located a few minutes away.
Thabo: “Its actually sewage from the Old pump station, at this point it’s dysfunctional, which is why all these ponds are actually filling up.
Phalaborwa’s municipality is upgrading their sewage system. They declined to comment. Just over 1 km downstream, the effluent flows into the jewel of our wildlife parks.
Link: This may look like just another example of pollution of raw sewage flowing over a large area of our countryside, but this is the Kruger National Park, and just imagine the effect on our wildlife.
Dr. Eddie Riddell manages the Olifants river within the Kruger National Park.

Eddie: “if you had smellovision your viewers would pick it up that it’s not too pleasant.”
He says the municipality must clean up its act as they are endangering the Kruger’s wildlife.
Eddie: “the phalaborwa waste water treatment works 10.18 that has the capacity of about 2-3 megalitre’s a day, phalaborwa are in the process of upgrading this plant to about 5 megalitre’s.”
The effects of the effluent can still be seen downstream. Water and Sanitation spokesperson Sputnik Ratau admits the department needs to better manage the Olifants and its polluters.
Question: The experts, say the government is not doing enough?
Sputnik: Is it ever enough? I don’t think so; you know delivery of services,
can never come to an optimum.
Question: We’re talking about a string of sewage works not operating or malfunctioning in some way?
Sputnik: I believe things have improved.
Question: Surely not along the Olifants Sputnik?
Sputnik: The Olifants is part of what we are still working around.
Sharon Pollard, executive Director of AWARD and an experienced water legislation and policy expert, says the biggest challenge is monitoring the mines that surround Phalaborwa.
Residents have nicknamed this area “Mordor”. It’s near the Olifants’ river and shows the impact of mining activity and settling dams.
Sharon: “Selati flows into kruger and then into selati, so we export our problems to Mazambique.”
Eddie: “About 2 years ago we had a big spill emanating from one of the industry associated with the mining complex.”
In January 2014, Phosphoric acid leaked into the Ga-Selati river from a fertilizer plant, and dropped the PH to one.
Thabo: “so you can literally run your car battery with it.
The Phosphate mine responsible was fined R2,55 million. Sputnik admits the department isn’t sufficiently monitoring mining activities.
Question: “We can tighten up in this area?”
Sputnik: “Yes we can, and we should.”
This SANPARKS report shows how hundreds of crocodiles have, since 2008, died from a painful disease called Pansteatitis.
Eddie: “There is a build up of fatty acids in fish, upon which the crocodiles then consume, and then the fatty acid buildup in the crocodile tissue.”
This buildup causes a rubber like hardening of fat reserves resulting in paraylsis and death from starvation. Dr. Riddell voiced concerns that cases of Pansteatitis may spike when the summer rains come and wash more pollutants into the park’s water.
An app developed by AWARD shows the state of the river, almost in real time.
Sharon: “We’ve now developed what we call a flow tracker and we’re expanding it to include water quality. you can know right here what the flow is and what the water quality conditions are, and that’s a first.”
Question: And you feel the situation is improving?
31:58
Sputnik: I believe that, maybe not along the Olifants at the moment but it is improving and obviously the Olifants is one of those critical ones that we need to look at very soon.
Sputnik has invited us to return next year to show us the department’s progress in dealing with the serious issues we have highlighted.
16:23
Paul: “It’s definitely not doom and gloom there’s a lot of initiatives going on in the Olifants catchment to improve the catchment.”
Sharon: “I think if anything that drives us as a species, as humanity it’s about thinking about our children and our children’s children. Future generations.”
There are examples of clean-up efforts upstream like in Burgersfort where the nappy build up has litterally cut off the flow.
Link: Nappies, nappies and even more nappies, they are littered everywhere, I’m standing in the Steelpoort river bed, and this flows into the Oliphant’s, there’s one man whose determined to clean this up. He grew up in the area, and his name is Peter Mashile.
Peter:”I have a passion, If I see waste lying around, my heart bleeds. I don’t like that.”
Studying theology opened Peter’s eyes to the wonders of nature. He put local mothers to work, washing and drying the nappies to be re-used, and the water disposed of properly.
Peter: “I can’t just watch my people die, we are helping our people, we are helping our river.
Peter’s nappy project enjoys wide support from cattle farmers like Daniel Phogo.
Derek: “Daniel, you had 22 head of cattle and now only 4, what happened?”
Daniel: “I found a full bundle of pampers inside the cow, and that material, it can’t digest the nappies.”
Cow dung shows the remnants of the nappies eaten. The river is less than a kilometer away. Daniel worries for his family as they have no other option but to drink the groundwater, which could be contaminated by ecoli.
Derek: “What about children who play in that water and I’m sure some of the people drink it?
Daniel: “No they are not thinking about whether it will make them sick, what they are focussing on is if they can get anything to eat so that they can survive.”
Derek: This is your passion and you’ve got no funding for it?
Peter: “No not at all, just doing it for the love of the environment.”
Peter believes his small contributions will make a big impact.
Peter: “I just want to encourage the love of nature. I’m an agent of change, I feel it in my heart.”
